name: Chloe Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Chloe Santos, 43, a senior operator at a large mine. I check the loader and road conditions, then move ore and brief the next crew; people call me when the machine starts shaking in a way they cannot place.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what gets tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like passing on what I know, especially to a new operator who is nervous around heavy equipment. The shifts are long, and my partner Daniel and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, though we have a few months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, use a small tool for reports if it gives us more time to check the loader. I would not want a screen to replace a walk around the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is mostly on the equipment, so a little paperwork help does not change my shift much. I still think the company can use small savings as an excuse to squeeze staffing, and that worries me more than the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current inspection routine and ask the planner to show us what the new report tool changes. I would leave our savings where they are and talk with my union steward if the mine reduced crew numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the job itself looks steady in this picture, but management can still change hours. The mortgage is covered today, and I do not want to spend our reserve over a small tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel if the mine cut one shift a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Daniel the rota and check whether the cut was temporary before changing the children's plans. We could pause the patio repair without dipping into the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a new report tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the maintenance team to compare its fault list with what they find on the loader. If the tool misses a warning, I would want a worker to sign off before it reaches the next shift.

say: A small tool can help with **reports** if it leaves more time for checks.
A screen should not replace a **walk around** the machine.
think: My work is mostly **hands-on**, so a little paperwork help changes little.
I worry that managers could use small savings to **squeeze staffing**.
do: Keep my **inspection routine** and ask what the report tool changes.
Talk with my **union steward** if the mine reduces crew numbers.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because the job looks steady but hours can still change.
S0.quote: I would not want a screen to replace a walk around the machine.
fieldNote: Chloe separates paperwork savings from the **equipment work** she values.
Her concern is management's possible **staffing response**, not the tool alone.
She has a few months of savings and would use **union representation** if hours fell.

steps.text: Keep the loader inspection routine on every shift
Ask the union steward about any crew reduction

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that software will take over some planning and checks, but it cannot yet load the ore. We should have a say in how the new targets are set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do shift handovers and help plan equipment checks, so part of my lead work could move quickly. The physical work stays longer, but I could lose some senior hours before any robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to review the new shift targets and attend the mine's paid safety inspection course. I would learn the report screen only after a trainer showed how to question a bad result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about the paperwork but anxious about losing lead hours. My work is still mainly physical, yet a cut to my shifts would touch our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the household budget would you protect first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the mortgage and children's school costs current, then postpone our bathroom update. Daniel and I would compare the rota with our monthly bills before spending from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course if the mine offered one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the paid safety course if it teaches checks that the mine still needs people to do. I would ask the trainer what happens to those inspection tasks as robots improve.

say: Software may take **planning and checks**, but it cannot yet load ore.
Workers should have a **say** in new shift targets.
think: Some lead tasks could move quickly, including **handover planning**.
I could lose senior **hours** before robots arrive.
New targets can change the **mortgage budget** even before robots arrive.
do: Ask the union to review new **shift targets**.
Attend the paid **safety inspection course** and question its future value.
feel: I am uneasy about paperwork and **anxious** about losing lead hours.
S1.quote: The physical work stays longer, but I could lose some senior hours before any robots arrive.
fieldNote: Her **planning duties** face change before the loader work.
Chloe wants a worker voice in **target setting** and course design.
She questions whether inspection skills remain useful as **robots improve**.

steps.text: Ask the union to review mine shift targets
Attend the mine's paid safety inspection course
Learn the report screen with a trainer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the scheduling and reports could change in 2028, but robots for the loader work follow around 2031. The mine should not use the short warning to make operators compete against one another for the remaining shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead a crew, so the planning part of my job is exposed right away. My hands-on work lasts longer, but I could still lose income when the thinking tools reduce the number of shifts before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for a written transfer and training plan now, before AGI arrives in 2028. In 2029, I would take the mine's paid inspection course if it leads to work that still requires a person to check equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not much time for a household to adjust, even with several months saved. I feel anxious because the three-year robot lag protects the loader work only temporarily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to put in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for advance notice, paid course places and a fair way to transfer senior operators. I would want the mine to say plainly whether the inspection jobs are expected to remain after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no course place is available in 2029, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the loader and ask to shadow the maintenance crew during a scheduled inspection. I would not resign or use our savings for a private course without knowing whether it leads to a job.

say: Scheduling may change by **2028**, while loader robots follow around 2031.
Do not make operators **compete** for the remaining shifts.
think: My crew planning is exposed as soon as **AGI** arrives.
Thinking tools could reduce my income before robots affect **loader work**.
do: Ask the union now for a written **transfer plan**.
Take a paid inspection course in 2029 if it leads to **human work**.
feel: Two years is short, and the robot lag protects my work only **temporarily**.
S2.quote: I feel anxious because the three-year robot lag protects the loader work only temporarily.
fieldNote: Chloe seeks a collective transfer plan before thinking AI changes **lead duties**.
She treats the robot lag as temporary protection, not a guaranteed **career**.
Several months of **savings** allow preparation but do not remove income risk.

steps.text: Ask the union for written transfer and training terms
Take the paid inspection course if it leads to a job
Keep operating while waiting for a confirmed course place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to bargain over training before AGI arrives in 2031. The loader work has roughly three more years after that, but I would not call the job safe until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift planning and reports may be automated first, while the physical work follows later. I could train for inspection, but robots may eventually handle those checks too, so I need an honest answer about how long that path lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete the mine's paid inspection course over the next few years and use the union to ask for a job transition agreement. In 2032, I would apply for a human inspection post if the mine still has one, while keeping my loader shifts until there is a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me more room to prepare than the fast version, but I remain anxious about what happens when robots reach the equipment. My experience counts for something, though I cannot assume it protects a job forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather train for inspection or leave mining altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try inspection first because I know the machines and the mine can pay for the course. I would also ask the union which nearby industries value safety experience, in case the mine has no lasting post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the time before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we are using the next five years to prepare, not waiting for a machine to decide our future. I would encourage them to choose training that has employers outside this mine.

say: Five years gives us time to bargain before AGI arrives in **2031**.
Loader work has three more years, but is not **safe** until 2034.
think: Planning may go first, while hands-on work changes **later**.
Inspection may help for a time, but robots could take those **checks** too.
do: Complete the paid **inspection course** and seek a union transition agreement.
Apply in 2032 for a human post while keeping **loader shifts**.
feel: I remain **anxious** about the robot arrival despite having more time.
S3.quote: I could train for inspection, but robots may eventually handle those checks too, so I need an honest answer about how long that path lasts.
fieldNote: She does not treat inspection as a protected career because of possible **robot takeover**.
Chloe combines paid **training** with collective bargaining for a transition.
She would look beyond mining if the site offers no **durable post**.

steps.text: Complete the mine's paid inspection course
Ask the union for a written transition agreement
Apply for the human inspection post in 2032 if the mine has a vacancy
Keep loader shifts until a new offer is written

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to plan if managers share dates and pay for training. AGI in 2036 changes the reports first, while robots around 2039 put the physical work at risk later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when robots follow, so I will still need a job. I can train toward inspections, but I know that work may not last if machines learn to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the mine's inspection course before 2036 and ask for a written transition plan. In 2037, I would apply for a human inspection post if one still exists, while keeping my current work until the offer is firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years make planning feel possible, but I am not reassured about work after 2039. Our savings can buy some time, not replace wages for a long stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your family still be making the same plans by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, our children will be young adults, though the mortgage may still be with us. Daniel and I would help them compare training for work across several industries, not assume our mine will employ them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before moving to another town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a signed offer and a clear housing budget before moving. Some similar jobs are nearby, so I would compare those first rather than uproot the family for a guess.

say: A decade is enough to plan if managers share **dates** and pay for training.
Reports change first; robots later put **physical work** at risk.
think: At 53 and 56 I will still need **work**.
Inspection is a path to try, not a **lasting guarantee**.
do: Apply in 2037 for an inspection post while keeping my **current work**.
feel: The extra years help planning, but I am not reassured about **work after 2039**.
S4.quote: Our savings can buy some time, not replace wages for a long stretch.
fieldNote: The longer lead time lets her train while staying in **paid work**.
She expects today's school-age children to be young adults by **2037**.
She would compare **local jobs** before moving the family.

steps.text: Complete the mine inspection course before 2036
Keep current work until a firm inspection offer arrives
Apply for a human inspection post in 2037
Help young adult children compare training across industries

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because it cuts the time for training before work changes. Paid courses, a union-backed transfer plan and clear notice about which posts remain would help our family plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want a worker representative in the room when the mine sets automation plans. A training certificate should connect to a real job, or it is just another cost for workers to carry.

headlineQuote: A training certificate should connect to a real job, or it is just another cost for workers to carry.
portrait: Chloe is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a **technical diploma**.
She is cautious with new technology and values **worker safety** and union voice.
Her partner and two children share a mortgage, with **several months saved**.
She seeks paid training but remains unsure whether **robots** will take inspection work too.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her because it leaves little time to arrange training and transfers.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **courses**, a union-backed transfer plan and clear staffing dates would help her prepare.
